posts.post_title: Who reported the serological grouping of str…
posts.post_content: Who first reported a serological method of grouping streptococci based on the carbohydrate (C) antigen of the cell wall?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rebecca Lancefield

In 1928, Rebecca Lancefield devised the serological grouping of streptococci.

Correct Option Explanation

Lancefield's scheme (finalised in 1933) classified beta-haemolytic streptococci into groups A-U (except I and J) based on the cell-wall carbohydrate (C) antigen.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hugo Schottmuller (1903) introduced blood agar to differentiate types of haemolysis, not serogrouping.
  • Pasteur (1878-79) recognised streptococci as a pus-forming agent.
  • Rivolta (1873) first described chain-forming organisms from strangles pus in horses.
Know More
  • Brown (1919) classified streptococci by haemolysis type on horse blood agar.
  • Alpha-haemolytic streptococci are also called viridans streptococci.
  • S. agalactiae belongs to Lancefield group B.
  • 19 Lancefield groups have been identified so far.

posts.post_title: Which Lancefield group does S. agalactiae be…
posts.post_content: Streptococcus agalactiae, the causal agent of chronic bovine mastitis, belongs to which Lancefield serological group?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Group B

S. agalactiae is a Lancefield group B streptococcus.

Correct Option Explanation

It causes chronic mastitis in cattle, sheep and goats, and neonatal septicaemia in humans and dogs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Group A is the group of S. pyogenes, associated with scarlet fever and rheumatic fever in humans.
  • Group C includes S. dysgalactiae and S. equi, causing acute mastitis and strangles respectively.
  • Group D includes enterococci such as S. faecalis, associated with opportunistic infections.
Know More
  • CAMP test is used to identify group B streptococci.
  • S. agalactiae produces bluish-grey colonies on Edward's medium.
  • Group A streptococci carry the M protein virulence factor.
  • Group B capsules are polysaccharide in nature.

posts.post_title: Cause of strangles in young horses
posts.post_content: Which organism is the principal cause of strangles, a disease of young horses characterised by catarrhal nasal discharge and pharyngeal lymph node abscessation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Streptococcus equi subsp. equi

S. equi subsp. equi causes strangles in young horses.

Correct Option Explanation

Infection spreads through lymph channels causing abscessation of pharyngeal lymph nodes; a serious sequel is purpura haemorrhagica, an immune-mediated disease appearing 1-3 weeks after illness.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • S. uberis is a Lancefield ungroupable species causing bovine mastitis, not strangles.
  • S. suis causes meningitis and arthritis in pigs, particularly young piglets.
  • S. canis causes neonatal septicaemia and skin/wound infections in carnivores.
Know More
  • 'Bastard strangles' refers to abscesses in multiple internal organs.
  • S. equi subsp. zooepidemicus causes mastitis, abortion and pneumonia in horses.
  • Strangles spreads via lymphatic channels from the nasal mucosa.
  • M, T and R proteins provide type specificity in group A/C streptococci.

posts.post_title: Streptolysin responsible for beta-haemolysis…
posts.post_content: Which streptococcal haemolysin, being oxygen-stable, is responsible for the beta-haemolysis seen around colonies on the surface of blood agar plates?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Streptolysin S

Streptolysin S is oxygen-stable and causes visible surface beta-haemolysis on blood agar.

Correct Option Explanation

It is soluble in serum (hence 'S'); it is a protein but is not antigenic, and is shown experimentally to be nephrotoxic.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Streptolysin O is oxygen-labile, seen only in pour plates, and is antigenic with cardiotoxic activity.
  • Streptokinase (fibrinolysin) lyses fibrin clots by activating plasminogen, not a haemolysin.
  • Streptodornase depolymerises DNA in pyogenic exudates, unrelated to haemolysis.
Know More
  • ASO titre estimation aids retrospective diagnosis of S. pyogenes infection.
  • Streptolysins O and S are produced by groups A, C and G.
  • Hyaluronidase breaks down hyaluronic acid of tissues.
  • Four antigenically distinct streptodornases (A-D) are recognised.

posts.post_title: Test differentiating S. pyogenes from other …
posts.post_content: Sensitivity to which antibiotic is used as a convenient laboratory method to differentiate Streptococcus pyogenes from other haemolytic streptococci?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bacitracin

Sensitivity to bacitracin differentiates S. pyogenes from other haemolytic streptococci.

Correct Option Explanation

S. pyogenes is more resistant to crystal violet but susceptible to sulphonamides and antibiotics, and specifically sensitive to bacitracin, an easy diagnostic marker.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Optochin sensitivity distinguishes S. pneumoniae from other alpha-haemolytic (viridans) streptococci.
  • Novobiocin resistance is used to differentiate certain staphylococcal species, not streptococci here.
Know More
  • Streptococci are catalase and oxidase negative.
  • S. pyogenes is destroyed by heat at 54°C for 30 minutes.
  • The pneumococcus-viridans differentiation also uses the bile solubility test.
  • Streptococci are not soluble in 10% bile, unlike pneumococci.

posts.post_title: Aesculin-hydrolysing selective medium for st…
posts.post_content: Which selective medium, containing blood agar, crystal violet and aesculin, is used to differentiate streptococcal species based on aesculin hydrolysis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Edward's medium

Edward's medium differentiates streptococcal species by ability to hydrolyse aesculin.

Correct Option Explanation

On this medium, inoculated secretions from mastitis give distinctive colonies: S. agalactiae produces bluish-grey colonies and S. uberis produces dark-coloured colonies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mannitol Salt agar is selective for Staphylococcus due to high salt tolerance, not streptococci.
  • MacConkey agar is not grown on by most streptococci, except Enterococcus faecalis.
  • Bird seed agar is selective for Cryptococcus neoformans, a fungal pathogen.
Know More
  • Ability to grow in 0.1% tellurite broth is characteristic of S. faecalis.
  • S. pneumoniae forms 'draughtsman colonies' on blood agar after 48-72 hrs.
  • Virulent streptococcal strains form matt (finely granular) colonies.
  • CAMP test uses staphylococcal beta toxin to identify group B streptococci.

posts.post_title: Peptostreptococcus indolicus and summer mast…
posts.post_content: Peptostreptococcus indolicus, an anaerobic streptococcus, is responsible for summer mastitis in cattle in association with which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Arcanobacterium pyogenes

Peptostreptococcus indolicus together with Arcanobacterium pyogenes causes summer mastitis in cattle.

Correct Option Explanation

The mixed anaerobic-aerobic infection produces thick, foul-smelling purulent secretion typical of summer mastitis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Fusobacterium necrophorum is a distinct anaerobe associated with foot rot and necrotic conditions, not the classical summer mastitis partner here.
  • Staphylococcus aureus causes gangrenous and chronic bovine mastitis independently.
  • Mycoplasma bovis causes contagious bovine mastitis unrelated to this anaerobic association.
Know More
  • S. agalactiae, S. dysgalactiae and S. uberis are the classical mastitis streptococci.
  • Chronic insidious mastitis is typical of S. agalactiae and S. uberis.
  • S. dysgalactiae causes sudden-onset acute single-quarter mastitis.
  • CAMP test (1944) is named after Christie, Atkins, Munch and Peterson.

posts.post_title: Cause of porcine cervical lymphadenitis
posts.post_content: Which streptococcal species causes porcine cervical lymphadenitis and is also isolated from meningitis, arthritis and endocarditis in pigs?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Streptococcus suis

S. suis causes porcine cervical lymphadenitis in pigs.

Correct Option Explanation

It also causes meningitis, arthritis, septicaemia, endocarditis and erosive arthritis in young pigs; S. suis type 1 affects pigs 2-4 weeks old and type 2 affects pigs 4-6 months old.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • S. porcinus (Lancefield P, U, V) causes jowl abscesses and lymphadenitis, a distinct pig pathogen.
  • S. canis primarily affects carnivores, causing neonatal septicaemia and wound infections.
  • S. gallinarum causes acute septicaemia with peritonitis in chickens, not pigs.
Know More
  • S. suis type 2 is a recognised zoonotic pathogen causing human meningitis.
  • Lactococcus lactis is isolated from cattle with unknown disease significance.
  • Enterococcus faecalis causes opportunistic infections in many species.
  • M protein of S. pyogenes is acid and heat labile.

posts.post_title: Chain formation mechanism in streptococci
posts.post_content: What is the primary cause of chain formation in streptococci?

_aimcq_options.text: Cocci dividing in one plane with daughter cells failing to separate
Presence of a hyaluronic acid capsule
Formation of L-forms after penicillin exposure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cocci dividing in one plane with daughter cells failing to separate

Chain formation results from cocci dividing in one plane only, with daughter cells not separating completely.

Correct Option Explanation

Each coccus is about 1 µm in diameter; streptococci are Gram-positive, non-motile and non-spore forming.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The hyaluronic acid capsule is a virulence factor inhibiting phagocytosis, unrelated to chain morphology.
  • L-forms (protoplasts) are induced by penicillin or phage-associated lysin and propagated on hypertonic media, not related to chain formation.
  • Streptokinase is a fibrinolytic enzyme, not related to cell division pattern.
Know More
  • Streptococci are facultative anaerobes.
  • Capsulation is not a regular feature of streptococci.
  • Group B and D streptococci commonly have polysaccharide capsules.
  • S. pyogenes and some group C strains bear hyaluronic acid capsules.

posts.post_title: Who first named the genus Staphylococcus?
posts.post_content: Which surgeon first discovered and named the genus Staphylococcus in 1880, after observing it in infected tissues?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alexander Ogston

Scottish surgeon Sir Alexander Ogston named the genus in 1880.

Correct Option Explanation

The name derives from Greek staphyle (bunch of grapes) and kokkas (berry), reflecting the grape-cluster arrangement on agar media.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Robert Koch is known for his postulates and discovery of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, not Staphylococcus.
  • Louis Pasteur recognised streptococci as a pus-forming agent in 1878-79.
  • Rebecca Lancefield devised streptococcal serogrouping in 1928, unrelated to Staphylococcus naming.
Know More
  • Staphylococcal cells are 0.8-1 µm in diameter.
  • They occur as small groups, pairs or short chains of up to four members in broth.
  • Species of veterinary importance include S. intermedius and S. hyicus.
  • Staphylococcus colonises the nasal cavity, skin and mucous membranes.

posts.post_title: Salt tolerance and Staphylococcus culture
posts.post_content: Staphylococcus can grow in the presence of what concentration of sodium chloride, making salt-containing media selective for it?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 7-10%

Staphylococcus tolerates 7-10% sodium chloride, the basis of Mannitol Salt agar selectivity.

Correct Option Explanation

This salt level is highly inhibitory to many other bacteria, particularly Gram-negative organisms, making the medium selective.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1-2% and 3-5% salt concentrations do not provide adequate selectivity against competing flora.
  • 15-20% salt exceeds the tolerance typically cited for staphylococcal selective media.
Know More
  • Optimum growth temperature for Staphylococcus is 35-37°C.
  • Purple agar with bromocresol purple and 1% maltose differentiates S. aureus and S. intermedius.
  • Hot-cold lysis phenomenon is seen on sheep/rabbit blood agar.
  • Death of staphylococci occurs at 60°C for 30 minutes.

posts.post_title: Antigen present only in S. aureus among stap…
posts.post_content: Which cell-wall antigen is present specifically in Staphylococcus aureus and not in S. intermedius?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Protein A

Protein A is present only in S. aureus.

Correct Option Explanation

Group antigens also include ribitol teichoic acid in S. aureus cell walls, whereas S. intermedius contains glycerol teichoic acid instead.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ribitol teichoic acid is present in S. aureus cell walls but is not exclusive in the way Protein A is described; it is a group carbohydrate antigen.
  • Glycerol teichoic acid is a feature of S. intermedius, not S. aureus.
  • Peptidoglycan is a general cell-wall component of all Gram-positive bacteria, not species-specific.
Know More
  • Type antigens are proteins other than Protein A.
  • Capsule and teichoic acid confer antiphagocytic ability.
  • Four antigenically distinct haemolysins exist: alpha, beta, delta, epsilon.
  • Alpha toxin is the major toxin in gangrenous mastitis.

posts.post_title: Cause of exudative epidermitis (greasy pig d…
posts.post_content: Exudative epidermitis, also known as greasy pig disease, an acute generalized infection of suckling and weaned pigs, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Staphylococcus hyicus

S. hyicus causes exudative epidermitis (greasy pig disease).

Correct Option Explanation

The disease is characterised by excess sebaceous secretion, exfoliation and exudation in suckling and weaned pigs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • S. aureus causes bovine mastitis and botryomycosis, not exudative epidermitis in pigs.
  • S. intermedius causes canine pyoderma and otitis externa in dogs and cats.
  • S. epidermidis is generally a coagulase-negative commensal, not the causative species named for this pig disease.
Know More
  • S. aureus subsp. anaerobius causes caseous lymphadenitis and is catalase negative.
  • Bumble foot is a pyogranulomatous foot infection in poultry.
  • Omphalitis is yolk-sac infection in turkeys/poultry.
  • Tick pyaemia in lambs is linked to Ixodes ricinus infestation.

posts.post_title: Test used to detect free coagulase of Staphy…
posts.post_content: Which test detects free coagulase (staphylocoagulase) secreted by Staphylococcus into plasma, shown by clot formation after incubation at 37°C for 24 hours?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Tube coagulase test

The tube coagulase test detects free coagulase secreted into plasma.

Correct Option Explanation

It is the definitive test for coagulase production; a positive result is clot formation after 24 hrs incubation at 37°C.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The slide coagulase test detects bound coagulase (clumping factor), shown by clumping within 1-2 minutes, a different mechanism.
  • The CAMP test identifies group B streptococci using staphylococcal beta toxin, unrelated to coagulase.
  • The Hotis test is used on milk samples for CPS detection, producing greenish-brown colonies with white centres, not a plasma clotting test.
Know More
  • CPS stands for coagulase-positive staphylococci, considered significant pathogens.
  • Phage typing is used epidemiologically for S. aureus bovine mastitis strains.
  • Coagulase is heat resistant.
  • Coagulation of plasma forms a fibrin film that aids bacterial multiplication.

posts.post_title: Enterotoxin heat resistance in Staphylococcu…
posts.post_content: Staphylococcal enterotoxins responsible for food poisoning in man are notable for which property?

_aimcq_options.text: They are heat-stable, not destroyed at 100°C for 30 minutes
They require living host cells to act
They are produced only by coagulase-negative strains

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: They are heat-stable, not destroyed at 100°C for 30 minutes

Staphylococcal enterotoxins are heat stable and survive 100°C for 30 minutes.

Correct Option Explanation

Several antigenically distinct enterotoxin types exist; they are seldom produced by animal strains but are the cause of human food poisoning.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The claim that they are destroyed rapidly at 60°C is false; their defining feature is heat stability.
  • Enterotoxins act as preformed toxins ingested with food, not requiring living host cells for their toxic action.
  • Enterotoxins are produced by toxigenic strains regardless of coagulase status, not restricted to coagulase-negative strains.
Know More
  • Exfoliative toxin causes skin necrosis by exfoliation.
  • TSST (toxic shock syndrome toxin) induces excess lymphokine production.
  • Both bovine and human strains of S. aureus can produce TSST.
  • Leukotoxin includes alpha and delta toxins with leukocidal activity.

posts.post_title: Selective medium differentiating S. aureus a…
posts.post_content: Which medium, containing bromocresol purple as a pH indicator and 1% maltose, is used to differentiate S. aureus from S. intermedius?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Purple agar

Purple agar, containing bromocresol purple and 1% maltose, differentiates S. aureus from S. intermedius.

Correct Option Explanation

Differential fermentation of maltose changes the indicator colour, distinguishing the two species.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mannitol Salt agar is selective for Staphylococcus via high salt tolerance, not specifically for maltose-based species differentiation.
  • Phenolphthalein diphosphate/tellurite agar selectively inhibits non-pathogenic strains rather than distinguishing S. aureus from S. intermedius.
Know More
  • S. aureus colonies are golden/yellow-orange pigmented.
  • S. albus forms white colonies; S. citreus forms lemon-yellow colonies.
  • Pigment-based classification was later abandoned as pigmentation is variable.
  • Staphylococcus can liberate 'V' factor, aiding Haemophilus growth.

posts.post_title: Botryomycosis in horses and cattle
posts.post_content: Chronic granulomatous lesions involving the udder of the mare, cow and sow, or the spermatic cord of horses, caused by Staphylococcus, are known as?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Botryomycosis

Botryomycosis refers to infrequent chronic granulomatous staphylococcal lesions of the udder or spermatic cord.

Correct Option Explanation

It classically involves the udder of mares, cows and sows, and the spermatic cord in horses (post-castration).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bumble foot is a pyogranulomatous process of the subcutaneous tissue of the foot in poultry, not udder/spermatic cord lesions.
  • Pyoderma is a common skin disease of dogs, distinct from the deep granulomatous lesions of botryomycosis.
  • Omphalitis is yolk-sac infection in poultry, unrelated to udder or spermatic cord lesions.
Know More
  • Periorbital eczema is a staphylococcal dermatitis in sheep from abrasions.
  • Gangrenous mastitis in postparturient cows is toxin-mediated.
  • Wing rot is a gangrenous dermatitis infection in poultry.
  • MRSA denotes methicillin-resistant S. aureus.

posts.post_title: Who first isolated the anthrax bacillus in p…
posts.post_content: Who is credited with first isolating the anthrax bacillus in pure culture in 1863?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Koch

Koch (1863) was the first to isolate the anthrax bacillus in pure culture.

Correct Option Explanation

Anthrax bacteriology has a rich history: Pollender (1849) first observed it microscopically; Davaine (1850) showed it was transmissible by blood inoculation; Pasteur (1881) prepared the first attenuated vaccine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pasteur (1881) is credited with preparing the attenuated anthrax vaccine, not with pure culture isolation.
  • Pollender (1849) was the first to observe the anthrax bacillus under the microscope, a pathogenic bacterium first seen.
  • Davaine (1850) demonstrated the first communicable disease transmissible by inoculation of infected blood.
Know More
  • Discovery of the anthrax bacillus is credited to Davaine and Rayer (1863-1868).
  • B. anthracis measures 4-8 µm × 1-1.5 µm.
  • Chains of bacilli show a bamboo stick (box-car) appearance.
  • The capsule is composed of a polymer of D-glutamic acid.

posts.post_title: Component of the extracellular toxin of B. a…
posts.post_content: Protective humoral antibodies against Bacillus anthracis develop mainly against which toxin component?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Factor II (protective antigen)

Protective antibodies develop against Factor II, the protective antigen (PA), and last about one year.

Correct Option Explanation

They typically develop 7-10 days after exposure; the toxin complex includes Factor I (EF), Factor II (PA), and Factor III (LF), all essential together for toxicity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Factor I (oedema factor, EF) is a chelating compound with phosphorus, protein and carbohydrate moieties; it is not the primary protective-antibody target.
  • Factor III (lethal factor, LF) is a protein component contributing to toxicity, not the main immunogen described.
  • The capsular polypeptide (poly-D-glutamic acid) is antiphagocytic but is only detectable in virulent strains, not the protective-antibody target here.
Know More
  • Bail termed the active protective substances 'aggresins'.
  • The Sterne vaccine uses spores of a noncapsulated avirulent mutant strain.
  • The Mazucchi vaccine uses the carbazoo strain in 2% saponin.
  • Pasteur's vaccine was attenuated by growth at 42-43°C.

posts.post_title: Selective medium for isolating B. anthracis …
posts.post_content: Which selective medium, containing polymyxin, lysozyme, EDTA and thallous acetate, is used to isolate B. anthracis from mixtures of spore-bearing bacilli?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: PLET medium

PLET medium (Polymyxin, Lysozyme, EDTA, Thallous acetate) added to heart infusion agar is selective for B. anthracis.

Correct Option Explanation

It suppresses contaminating spore-bearing bacilli while allowing B. anthracis colonies to be recognised.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Edward's medium (blood agar, crystal violet, aesculin) is used for streptococcal differentiation, not B. anthracis.
  • Bird seed agar selects for Cryptococcus neoformans, a fungal pathogen.
  • Mannitol Salt agar is selective for Staphylococcus via high salt tolerance.
Know More
  • B. anthracis colonies show a frosted glass appearance on agar.
  • The serrated colony edge gives a medusa head / judge's wig appearance.
  • In gelatin stab culture, growth shows an inverted fir tree appearance.
  • Virulent capsulated strains form rough colonies, avirulent strains form smooth colonies.

posts.post_title: Ascoli's test for anthrax
posts.post_content: The Ascoli's precipitation test for anthrax, described in 1911, detects a positive reaction by which sign?

_aimcq_options.text: A white ring of precipitation at the interface

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A white ring of precipitation at the interface

Ascoli's test (1911) shows a white ring of precipitation at the interface of anti-anthrax serum and boiled organ filtrate.

Correct Option Explanation

The suspected organ/blood is ground, boiled, filtered, and the clear filtrate is overlaid on anti-anthrax serum (1:50); a positive ring forms within 15 minutes at room temperature.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Clot formation describes the coagulase test for Staphylococcus, an unrelated assay.
  • A colour change is not the readout of Ascoli's test, which relies on visible precipitation.
  • Clumping of cells describes agglutination-based tests, not the Ascoli precipitation reaction.
Know More
  • The String of Pearls test (Charlton, 1980) uses penicillin-containing tryptose agar.
  • Cherry gamma phage lysis is used to confirm B. anthracis identity.
  • B. anthracis strain 14 is used as the phage-test control.
  • Guinea pigs and mice are highly susceptible to experimental inoculation.

posts.post_title: Susceptibility of species to anthrax infecti…
posts.post_content: Among domestic animal species, which group is described as most susceptible to anthrax infection?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cattle, sheep and goats

Cattle, sheep and goats are most susceptible to anthrax.

Correct Option Explanation

Horses and humans occupy an intermediate susceptibility, while pigs and carnivores are comparatively resistant; birds are highly resistant overall.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pigs and carnivores are comparatively resistant, not the most susceptible group.
  • Horses and humans occupy an intermediate position, below cattle/sheep/goats in susceptibility.
  • Birds are highly resistant to anthrax, the opposite of the most susceptible group.
Know More
  • Bulls have a mortality rate of about 90% in bovine anthrax.
  • In peracute bovine septicaemia, death occurs within 2 hours.
  • Spleen in anthrax cases shows a 'black cherry jam' consistency.
  • Anthrax carcasses should not be opened; only a muzzle/ear piece is sent for testing.

posts.post_title: Stain used to demonstrate the anthrax capsul…
posts.post_content: Which stain is used on heat-fixed blood smears to demonstrate the characteristic dark pink/purple capsule of Bacillus anthracis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Polychrome methylene blue (McFadyean's reaction)

Staining with polychrome methylene blue reveals an amorphous purplish capsular material around B. anthracis, known as McFadyean's reaction.

Correct Option Explanation

This reaction's clarity depends on the degree of heat used for smear fixation; smears from horses/pigs should be made from oedematous fluid or lymph nodes due to fewer circulating organisms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Gram's stain demonstrates Gram-positive rods generally but does not specifically highlight the capsule as this reaction does.
  • Ziehl-Neelsen stain is an acid-fast stain used for Mycobacterium, not for anthrax capsule demonstration.
  • Plain Giemsa stain alone is used to view morphology but the specific capsular demonstration described is the polychrome methylene blue reaction.
Know More
  • B. anthracis spores do not stain by ordinary methods but can be stained with Sudan black B.
  • Sporulation never occurs in the living animal body.
  • Optimum sporulation temperature is 25-30°C.
  • Spores survive dry heat at 140°C for 2-3 hrs.

posts.post_title: Duckering process for wool disinfection agai…
posts.post_content: The process of disinfecting wool against anthrax spores using 2% formaldehyde at 39-40°C for 20 minutes is termed?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Duckering

This formaldehyde-based wool disinfection process is called duckering.

Correct Option Explanation

Animal hair and bristles are treated with 0.25% formaldehyde at 60°C for 6 hrs using the same principle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pasteurisation is a mild heat treatment for milk/liquids, an unrelated process for wool disinfection.
  • Tyndallisation is fractional sterilisation by repeated boiling, not the formaldehyde wool process described.
  • Autoclaving uses pressurised steam sterilisation, distinct from the chemical duckering process.
Know More
  • Anthrax spores can be killed at 120°C for 10 minutes.
  • 4% KMnO4 treatment for 15 minutes also kills spores.
  • Spores survive in 5% phenol for weeks.
  • Vegetative bacilli are destroyed at 60°C in 30 minutes.

posts.post_title: Emerging Bacillus species linked to abortion…
posts.post_content: Which emerging Bacillus pathogen is implicated in sporadic abortions in cattle and sheep, often linked to contaminated silage?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bacillus licheniformis

B. licheniformis is an emerging pathogen implicated in sporadic abortions in cattle and sheep.

Correct Option Explanation

Infection is associated with feeding of contaminated silage; its colonies show characteristic hair-like outgrowths and become brown with age, resembling lichen (source of its name).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • B. cereus causes food poisoning in humans and produces wide zones of complete haemolysis, not the silage-linked abortion syndrome.
  • B. subtilis is a non-pathogenic 'anthracoid' organism used mainly as a reference/contaminant species.
  • B. megaterium is likewise classified among the non-pathogenic anthracoid Bacillus species.
Know More
  • Non-pathogenic Bacillus species are collectively called anthracoids.
  • B. anthracis produces weak haemolysis compared with anthracoid strong haemolysis.
  • Anthracoid organisms are generally motile, unlike B. anthracis.
  • B. anthracis ferments salicin slowly, while anthracoids ferment it rapidly.

posts.post_title: Who first isolated C. tetani in pure culture?
posts.post_content: Who isolated Clostridium tetani in pure culture in 1889 and reproduced tetanus in animals by inoculation of the pure culture?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Kitasato

Kitasato (1889) isolated C. tetani in pure culture and reproduced tetanus by inoculation.

Correct Option Explanation

Rosenbach (1886) had earlier demonstrated a slender bacillus with round terminal spores in a tetanus case, laying groundwork for Kitasato's isolation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rosenbach (1886) demonstrated the organism microscopically but did not achieve pure culture isolation.
  • Hippocrates is credited with the earliest historical description of tetanus, long before its bacteriology was known.
  • Van Ermengem (1896) first isolated C. botulinum, not C. tetani.
Know More
  • The word 'tetanus' derives from the Greek for 'contracture'.
  • C. tetani produces a terminal spherical spore, giving a drumstick appearance.
  • Ten serotypes (I-X) of C. tetani exist based on flagellar antigen.
  • All types produce the same neurotoxin, tetanospasmin.

posts.post_title: Mode of action of tetanospasmin
posts.post_content: How does tetanospasmin, the neurotoxin of Clostridium tetani, exert its paralytic effect?

_aimcq_options.text: Peripherally by blocking neuromuscular transmission, causing flaccid paralysis
Centrally by blocking synaptic inhibition, causing spastic paralysis
By lysing red blood cells directly
By degrading tropomyosin in muscle fibres

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Centrally by blocking synaptic inhibition, causing spastic paralysis

Tetanospasmin acts centrally by blocking synaptic inhibition, producing spastic paralysis.

Correct Option Explanation

This contrasts with botulinum toxin, which acts peripherally by blocking neuromuscular transmission, causing flaccid paralysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis

  • Type A (e.g. A:5, A:8, A:9) causes fowl cholera, not atrophic rhinitis.

  • Carter's classification uses PHA to define capsular types A-F (C is invalid).

posts.post_title: Colonial form of Pasteurella that is complet…
posts.post_content: Which colonial form of Pasteurella multocida, lacking capsular or mucoid antigen, is completely avirulent for rabbits?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rough form

The rough form is completely avirulent for rabbits, giving a granular deposit in broth.

It has neither a capsular nor mucoid antigen, distinguishing it from the virulent smooth and intermediate mucoid forms.

  • The smooth form is virulent for rabbits and contains a type-specific polysaccharide capsular antigen — the opposite of avirulent rough form.
  • The mucoid form shows intermediate virulence and is rich in hyaluronic acid, not the avirulent extreme.

  • P. anatipestifer produces dewdrop colonies within 48 hrs.

posts.post_title: Person who first investigated Pasteurella mu…
posts.post_content: Pasteurella multocida was extensively investigated in 1880 as the cause of fowl cholera by whom?

  • Koch is associated with tuberculosis and anthrax bacteriology, not the fowl cholera investigation of Pasteurella.

posts.post_title: Basis of biotype differentiation of Mannheim…
posts.post_content: Mannheimia haemolytica (biotype A) and Pasteurella trehalosi (biotype T) are differentiated based on fermentation of which two sugars?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Arabinose and trehalose

Biotypes A and T are distinguished by fermentation of arabinose (biotype A) and trehalose (biotype T) respectively.

Serotypes 3, 4, 10 and 15 belong to biotype T (P. trehalosi); all other serotypes belong to biotype A (M. haemolytica).

posts.post_title: Meaning behind the genus name Haemophilus
posts.post_content: The genus name Haemophilus reflects the organism's requirement for which growth factors present in blood?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: X and V factors

Haemophilus ('blood-loving') requires one or both of the accessory growth factors X and V found in blood.

Correct Option Explanation

The X factor is heat-labile iron-porphyrin-haematin needed for catalase synthesis; the V factor is a heat-labile coenzyme (NAD/NADP) acting as a hydrogen acceptor.

  • O and H antigens are serological classification antigens (used e.g. in E. coli and Salmonella typing), not the blood-derived growth factors defining Haemophilus.
  • K and F antigens refer to capsular and fimbrial antigens, not the specific X/V growth factor requirement.
  • Mycobactin and glycerol are growth requirements specific to certain Mycobacterium species, unrelated to Haemophilus.

  • H. somnus requires neither X nor V factor.
  • Chocolate agar is the most suitable medium for Haemophilus isolation.

posts.post_title: Phenomenon demonstrating Haemophilus depende…
posts.post_content: The phenomenon where Haemophilus colonies grow larger near a streak of Staphylococcus aureus on blood agar is called?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Satellitism

This is called satellitism, demonstrating Haemophilus dependence on V factor released by staphylococcal growth.

Colonies of Haemophilus are large near the Staphylococcus streak (high V factor concentration) and smaller farther away.

  • The CAMP phenomenon describes enhancement of staphylococcal beta haemolysis by streptococcal/other bacterial factors, a distinct interaction from satellitism.
  • The Nagler reaction demonstrates C. perfringens lecithinase activity, unrelated to Haemophilus growth factors.
  • 'Hot-cold lysis' describes a staphylococcal haemolysis pattern seen on incubation/chilling, unrelated to the Haemophilus-Staphylococcus interaction described.
Know More
  • Levinthal's medium and Filde's agar also support Haemophilus isolation.
  • Haemophilus cells die within 2-3 days in culture due to autolysis.
  • Haemophilus is destroyed by heating at 55°C for 30 minutes.

posts.post_title: Cause of thromboembolic meningoencephalitis …
posts.post_content: Thromboembolic meningoencephalitis (TEME), also called 'sleepers', in cattle is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemophilus somnus

Haemophilus somnus causes thromboembolic meningoencephalitis (TEME, 'sleepers') in cattle.

It also causes pneumonia/pleurisy, arthritis, endometritis/abortion in cattle, and epididymitis/orchitis in rams.

  • H. parasuis causes Glasser's disease (polyserositis/meningitis) in young pigs, not cattle TEME.

posts.post_title: Cause of Glasser's disease in young pigs
posts.post_content: Glasser's disease, characterized by polyserositis and meningitis in young pigs, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemophilus parasuis

Haemophilus parasuis causes Glasser's disease (polyserositis and meningitis) in young pigs.

Post-mortem shows large fibrin deposits on serosal surfaces, fibrinous pericarditis, pleuritis and peritonitis; the disease often occurs concurrently with viral infections.

  • H. parasuis was first described by Glasser (1910).

posts.post_title: Cause of wooden tongue in cattle
posts.post_content: Wooden (timber) tongue, a chronic pyogranulomatous condition of the bovine tongue, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Actinobacillus lignieresii

Actinobacillus lignieresii causes bovine actinobacillosis (wooden/timber tongue).

Chronic pyogranulomatous lesions cause tongue enlargement and protrusion, interfering with feeding; pus contains soft grayish-white granules.

  • A. equuli causes sleepy foal disease in newborn foals, unrelated to bovine tongue disease.

  • A. lignieresii was isolated by Ligniers and Spitz (1902).

posts.post_title: Distinguishing club colonies from bacilli us…
posts.post_content: In Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stained smears of actinobacillosis lesions, how do the club-like processes and the bacilli differ in colour?

_aimcq_options.text: Club appears red, bacilli appear blue
Club appears blue, bacilli appear red

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Club appears red, bacilli appear blue

With ZN staining, the club appears red while the bacilli appear blue.

Both club forms and bacilli are Gram-negative, but this ZN colour differential helps distinguish the calcium-phosphate club structures from the central A. lignieresii rods.

posts.post_title: Growth factor requirement distinguishing Act…
posts.post_content: Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae biotype 1 requires which growth factor, while biotype 2 is independent of it?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: NAD

Biotype 1 of A. pleuropneumoniae requires NAD for growth, while biotype 2 is NAD-independent.

Twelve serotypes and two biotypes of A. pleuropneumoniae have been described, with capsule, LPS, outer membrane proteins and toxins contributing to pathogenicity.

  • Mycobactin is a growth requirement specific to Mycobacterium avium subsp. paratuberculosis, not A. pleuropneumoniae biotypes.

posts.post_title: Cause of sleepy foal disease
posts.post_content: Sleepy foal disease, an acute potentially fatal septicaemia of newborn foals, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Actinobacillus equuli

Actinobacillus equuli causes sleepy foal disease, an acute septicaemia of newborn foals.

Correct Option Explanation

Foals can be infected in utero or after birth via the umbilicus; affected foals are febrile and recumbent, with death usually in 1-2 days.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A. lignieresii causes wooden tongue in cattle, a chronic granulomatous disease unrelated to foal septicaemia.

  • A. seminis causes epididymitis in rams, unrelated to newborn foal disease.
Know More
  • A. equuli occurs as a commensal in the equine intestinal tract and mouth.

posts.post_title: Cause of epididymitis in young rams among Ac…
posts.post_content: Epididymitis in young rams, associated with abscesses and purulent discharge through scrotal fistulae, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Actinobacillus seminis

Actinobacillus seminis is a common cause of epididymitis in young rams.

Correct Option Explanation

The organism is found in the prepuce, and infection likely occurs via an ascending opportunistic route.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A. lignieresii causes wooden tongue in cattle, an unrelated organism and disease site.
  • A. equuli causes sleepy foal disease in horses, a different host species entirely.

  • A. suis is present in the tonsil and upper respiratory tract of healthy pigs.

posts.post_title: Cause of glanders in horses
posts.post_content: Glanders, a contagious chronic disease of horses characterized by tubercle-like nodules that break down into ulcers, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pseudomonas mallei

Pseudomonas mallei (Malleomyces mallei) causes glanders in horses, mules and donkeys.

Correct Option Explanation

Three forms occur: pulmonary, nasal, and cutaneous (farcy), the latter showing nodules that develop into hollow ulcers with yellow or oily pus.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • P. aeruginosa causes wound infections, mastitis and various suppurative conditions across species, not the specific equine glanders syndrome.
  • P. pseudomallei causes melioidosis (pseudoglanders), a related but distinct disease affecting horses, cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and dogs.

Know More

  • P. mallei is the only Pseudomonas species that is non-motile.

posts.post_title: Pigment unique to Pseudomonas aeruginosa
posts.post_content: Which bluish-green, chloroform-soluble pigment is unique to Pseudomonas aeruginosa and gives cultures their characteristic blue colour?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pyocyanin

Pyocyanin is unique to P. aeruginosa and dissolves in chloroform, giving the classic blue colour.

Correct Option Explanation

Other pigments include pyoverdin (greenish-yellow, water-soluble, fluorescin), pyorubin (red) and pyomelanin (dark brown/black), which are less commonly produced.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pyoverdin is water-soluble (not chloroform-soluble) and greenish-yellow, distinct from the specifically 'unique' pyocyanin.
  • Pyorubin is a less commonly produced red pigment, not the one described as unique and diagnostic for the species.
  • Pyomelanin is a less common dark brown/black pigment, not the classic diagnostic blue pigment.
Know More
  • P. aeruginosa colonies have a characteristic fruity, grape-like odour.
  • Cetrimide agar is the selective medium for P. aeruginosa.
  • P. aeruginosa is IMViC pattern -,-,-,+.
  • P. aeruginosa produces exotoxin A, elastase and protease as virulence factors.

posts.post_title: Test used to demonstrate hypersensitivity in…
posts.post_content: Which glycoprotein-based test is used to demonstrate delayed hypersensitivity developed after Pseudomonas mallei infection in horses?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mallein test

The Mallein test, using a glycoprotein extracted from P. mallei, demonstrates hypersensitivity from glanders infection.

Correct Option Explanation

It can be administered subcutaneously, ophthalmically, or intrapalpebrally, each producing characteristic local inflammatory reactions.

  • The Johnin test is the analogous delayed-hypersensitivity test for Johne's disease (M. avium subsp. paratuberculosis), not glanders.
  • The tuberculin test is used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis/bovis infection, an unrelated organism.

  • The Straus reaction in male guinea pigs is used for both P. mallei and P. pseudomallei, but is non-confirmatory.

posts.post_title: Cause of melioidosis (pseudoglanders)
posts.post_content: Melioidosis, also called pseudoglanders, affecting horses, cattle, sheep, goats, pigs and dogs, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pseudomonas pseudomallei

Pseudomonas pseudomallei (Whitmore's bacillus) causes melioidosis (pseudoglanders).

It was first described by Whitmore and Krishnaswamy (1912); it is mainly found in tropical soil, with wild rodents as an important reservoir.

  • P. mallei causes true glanders/farcy, a related but distinct disease primarily of equidae.

  • P. pseudomallei is peritrichous, unlike other motile Pseudomonas species which are polar-flagellated.

posts.post_title: Selective medium for isolation of Pseudomona…
posts.post_content: Which medium, containing cetrimide, is used as a selective medium for the isolation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cetrimide agar

Cetrimide agar is the selective medium for P. aeruginosa.

Correct Option Explanation

P. aeruginosa grows on a wide range of media including TSA and blood agar, but cetrimide provides selectivity for this species specifically.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Purple agar differentiates S. aureus from S. intermedius, unrelated to Pseudomonas selection.
  • PLET medium is selective for B. anthracis, an unrelated organism.

Know More
  • P. aeruginosa is resistant to heat only up to 55°C for one hour before being killed.

posts.post_title: Who first identified Brucella melitensis?
posts.post_content: Brucella melitensis was first identified by whom, in Malta, in 1887?

Correct Answer: Bruce

Bruce (1887) identified B. melitensis in Malta.

Bang (1897) recognised B. abortus, and Traum (1914) discovered B. suis; the genus name honours Bruce.

  • Bang (1897) is credited with recognising B. abortus, the cattle-associated species, not B. melitensis.

posts.post_title: Substance in the placenta favouring Brucella…
posts.post_content: Which substance, present in the placenta and male genital tract of cattle, sheep, goats and pigs but not humans, favours growth of most Brucella species?

  • Mycobactin is a growth requirement for M. avium subsp. paratuberculosis, an unrelated organism.

  • Abortion in cattle due to B. abortus typically occurs from 6 months of gestation onward.

posts.post_title: Species causing epididymitis in rams and abo…
posts.post_content: Which Brucella species, antigenically rough and lacking A/M antigens, causes epididymitis in rams and abortion in ewes?

Brucella ovis causes epididymitis in rams and abortion in ewes, and is always in the antigenically rough form.

posts.post_title: Live attenuated vaccine strain used against …
posts.post_content: Which live attenuated vaccine strain of Brucella abortus is used in female calves aged 4-12 months for brucellosis control?

Correct Answer: Strain 19

Strain 19 (B. abortus biotype 1) is the standard live attenuated vaccine used in female calves 4-12 months old.

posts.post_title: Most sensitive animal inoculation test for i…
posts.post_content: Which animal inoculation test, useful when material is badly contaminated or organism numbers are low, is the most sensitive method for isolating pathogenic Brucella?

Correct Answer: Straus reaction (guinea pig orchitis)

The Straus reaction — orchitis in male guinea pigs — is the most sensitive test for isolating pathogenic Brucella.

Guinea pigs are inoculated intramuscularly with tissue homogenate and euthanised 6 weeks later, with spleen and abnormal tissue collected for bacteriological examination.

posts.post_title: Cause of bovine genital campylobacteriosis (…
posts.post_content: Epizootic bovine infertility (bovine genital campylobacteriosis), transmitted venereally and causing early embryonic death, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Campylobacter fetus subsp. venerealis

C. fetus subsp. venerealis is an obligate parasite of bovine genitalia causing epizootic bovine infertility.

Infection is transmitted via coitus or artificial insemination; in bulls it is usually inapparent, while in cows it causes endometritis/salpingitis and infertility, with fertility usually regained within 5 months.

posts.post_title: Route of transmission for Campylobacter fetu…
posts.post_content: Unlike C. fetus subsp. venerealis, C. fetus subsp. fetus causes ovine abortion through which route of transmission?

C. fetus subsp. fetus enters via ingestion, causing bacteraemia and eventual placentitis and abortion near the end of gestation.

Venereal transmission does not occur with this subspecies, unlike C. fetus subsp. venerealis; infection in the first half of ovine gestation does not typically result in abortion.

  • Venereal (coitus) transmission is specific to C. fetus subsp. venerealis, not subsp. fetus, which is explicitly stated not to transmit venereally.

  • Mortality in ewes may exceed 5%.

posts.post_title: Biochemical test unique to Campylobacter jej…
posts.post_content: Which biochemical test result is unique to Campylobacter jejuni among Campylobacter species, showing a positive purple colour reaction?

Correct Answer: Hydrolysis of sodium hippurate

C. jejuni is the only Campylobacter species that hydrolyses sodium hippurate.

In this test, culture emulsified in sodium hippurate solution is incubated, then ninhydrin is added; a positive reaction gives a deep purple colour after 10 minutes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ehrlichia canis causes canine ehrlichiosis via tick transmission (Rhipicephalus sanguineus), not fish/fluke ingestion.
  • Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever, transmitted mainly by dust inhalation, unrelated to salmon ingestion.
  • Cowdria ruminantium causes heartwater in ruminants via Amblyomma ticks, an unrelated host and transmission route.
Know More
  • Neorickettsia targets reticular cells of lymphoid tissue.
  • The intermediate host cycle involves a snail for fluke development.
  • Diagnosis includes observing fluke eggs in faeces.
  • Also affected are foxes, bears and ferrets.

posts.post_title: Rickettsial species capable of growth on ord…
posts.post_content: Which rickettsial species is unique in having the ability to grow on ordinary blood agar, unlike other obligate intracellular Rickettsiales?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rochalimaea quintana

Rochalimaea quintana (cause of trench fever) is the only rickettsia able to grow on blood agar.

Correct Option Explanation

Most other Rickettsiales require living host cells (chicken embryo yolk sac or cell culture) for cultivation, since they are obligate intracellular parasites.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coxiella burnetii requires living cells for replication, though it is notably resistant in the environment as an endospore-like form; it does not grow on blood agar.
  • Rickettsia prowazekii (epidemic typhus) is an obligate intracellular organism requiring living cells, not blood agar growth.
  • Ehrlichia canis is best propagated in dog monocyte cell culture, not on blood agar.
Know More
  • Rickettsiae were first cultivated in chicken embryo yolk sac by Cox.
  • Rickettsiae have a 3-layered cell wall resembling Gram-negative bacteria.
  • They stain poorly with Gram's stain but well with Giemsa/Machiavello.
  • Machiavello stain gives a deep red appearance.

posts.post_title: Cell type targeted by Coxiella burnetii with…
posts.post_content: Coxiella burnetii, the causative agent of Q fever, primarily infects which cell type in the host?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Circulating leucocytes

Coxiella burnetii targets circulating leucocytes.

Correct Option Explanation

This differs from Ehrlichia and Cowdria, which target vascular endothelial cells, and from Rickettsia, which targets macrophages, leucocytes and endothelial cells.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vascular endothelial cells are the target of Ehrlichia and Cowdria, not Coxiella.
  • 'Macrophages and endothelial cells only' describes the broader tropism of genus Rickettsia, not the specific leucocyte tropism of Coxiella.
  • 'Reticular cells of lymphoid tissue' is the target of Neorickettsia, not Coxiella.
Know More
  • Q fever is transmitted to humans mainly by inhalation of contaminated dust.
  • Wild bandicoots may serve as a primary reservoir in some regions.
  • Transovarial transmission has been demonstrated in Ixodes ticks.
  • The flash pasteurisation method (not holding method) effectively kills C. burnetii in milk.

posts.post_title: Meaning of the term Chlamydia
posts.post_content: The term 'Chlamydia' is derived from a Greek word meaning what, referring to the appearance of inclusion bodies near infected cell nuclei?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mantle or cloak

'Chlamydia' derives from Greek 'chlamys', meaning mantle or cloak, describing the inclusion body appearance near the nucleus.

Correct Option Explanation

Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular parasites occupying a position intermediate between rickettsiae and viruses, sometimes called 'energy parasites' due to ATP dependence on the host.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Fungus' relates to the etymology of Mycobacterium ('fungus bacterium'), not Chlamydia.
  • 'Blood-loving' is the meaning behind the genus name Haemophilus, unrelated to Chlamydia.
  • 'Coil or spiral' describes the etymology of Spirochaetes (spira-chaite), not Chlamydia.
Know More
  • Chlamydia infection in psittacine birds is called psittacosis.
  • Infection in non-psittacine birds is called ornithosis.
  • Psittacosis agents are also called Bedsoniae, after Sir Samuel Bedson.
  • C. psittaci causes BUSS disease (sporadic bovine encephalomyelitis).

posts.post_title: Chlamydial developmental form responsible fo…
posts.post_content: Which developmental form of Chlamydia is small, spherical, and represents the infectious extracellular form of the organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Elementary body (EB)

The elementary body (EB), 200-300 nm in diameter, is the small, infectious extracellular form.

Correct Option Explanation

After entering a cell by endocytosis, EBs differentiate into the larger (500-1000 nm), metabolically active but non-infectious reticulate body (RB), which multiplies and later re-condenses into new EBs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The reticulate body is the non-infectious, intracellular, reproductive form — the opposite of the infectious EB described in the question.
  • 'Spherule' is a structure formed by Coccidioides immitis in tissue, an unrelated fungal organism.
  • 'Arthroconidium' is an asexual fungal spore type (e.g. in dermatophytes/Coccidioides), unrelated to Chlamydia's developmental cycle.
Know More
  • RBs mature into EBs at about 20 hours post-infection.
  • Infectious EB release occurs at about 40 hours post-infection via cell lysis.
  • Chlamydiae lack muramic acid in their cell wall, unlike typical Gram-negative bacteria.
  • They are inactivated within minutes at 56°C.

posts.post_title: Cause of enzootic abortion of ewes (EAE)
posts.post_content: Enzootic abortion of ewes, characterized by diffuse necrotic placentitis and abortion in the last 2-3 weeks of pregnancy, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chlamydophila (Chlamydia) psittaci

C. psittaci causes enzootic abortion of ewes (EAE), localizing in placental cells.

Correct Option Explanation

Unlike Campylobacter-induced abortion, which shows an autolysed foetus, EAE classically presents with a fresh foetus and diffuse necrotic placentitis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Campylobacter fetus subsp. fetus also causes ovine abortion but typically with an autolysed (decomposed) foetus, a key differential feature distinguishing it from EAE.
  • Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) can cause abortion in sheep/goats/cattle but is a distinct organism from Chlamydia with different transmission (dust inhalation).
  • Brucella ovis causes epididymitis in rams and abortion in ewes, but via a different pathogenic mechanism (rough antigenic Brucella species), not the classic Chlamydial EAE presentation.
Know More
  • Ovine/bovine Type 1 Chlamydia isolates are linked to abortion and genital infection.
  • Type II isolates cause conjunctivitis, pneumonia and polyarthritis.
  • Chlamydiae are highly sensitive to oxytetracycline.
  • Feline pneumonitis is diagnosed via Giemsa-stained conjunctival smears.

posts.post_title: Term for fungi that shift between mold and y…
posts.post_content: Fungi that exist in mycelial (mold) form at room temperature but convert to a yeast form at 37°C in animal tissue are termed?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dimorphic fungi

These are called dimorphic fungi, and the temperature-dependent shift is called the YM (Yeast-to-Mold) shift.

Correct Option Explanation

Examples include Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis and Sporothrix schenckii, which multiply as molds at 25°C and as yeasts at 37°C.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Monomorphic yeasts (e.g. Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans) multiply only by budding regardless of temperature, not shifting forms.
  • Monomorphic molds (e.g. Microsporum, Trichophyton, Aspergillus) multiply only via hyphal/spore growth, without a yeast phase.
  • Imperfect fungi (Deuteromycetes) refers to fungi lacking a demonstrable sexual reproduction stage, an unrelated classification concept from thermal dimorphism.
Know More
  • The optimum pH range for most fungal growth is 3.8 to 5.6.
  • Optimum growth temperature for saprophytic fungi is 22-30°C; for parasitic fungi, 30-37°C.
  • Obligate anaerobic fungi are found in the rumen of cattle.
  • The vegetative structure of a fungus is called the thallus.

posts.post_title: Type of spore formed by direct differentiati…
posts.post_content: Thick-walled, resistant asexual spores formed by direct differentiation of the mycelium, as seen in Candida albicans, are called?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chlamydospores

Chlamydospores are thick-walled, resistant spores formed by direct differentiation of the mycelium, as in Candida albicans.

Correct Option Explanation

They result from concentration of protoplasm and nutrients within a segment of hyphae, forming a resistant resting structure.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Arthrospores are formed by disarticulation of the mycelium (e.g. Geotrichum candidum), a different mechanism from direct differentiation.
  • Blastospores are produced by a budding process, as in Saccharomyces species, not by mycelial differentiation.
  • Sporangiospores are asexual spores produced within a closed sporangium structure (e.g. Rhizopus), a distinct spore-bearing mechanism.
Know More
  • Macroconidia are large, often multicellular conidia.
  • Microconidia are small, single-celled conidia.
  • Ascospores are sexual spores produced in a sac called an ascus.
  • Zygospores are thick-walled sexual spores of class Phycomycetes.

posts.post_title: Fungal class comprising the majority of path…
posts.post_content: Deuteromycetes (fungi imperfecti), the class comprising the majority of pathogenic fungi, are characterized by which feature?

_aimcq_options.text: Lack of a demonstrable means of sexual reproduction
Formation of broad, aseptate hyphae only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lack of a demonstrable means of sexual reproduction

Deuteromycetes lack a demonstrable sexual reproduction stage and are therefore considered 'imperfect'.

Correct Option Explanation

They are represented by filamentous (mold) and imperfect yeast forms, producing asexual thallospores (arthrospores, blastospores, chlamydospores) and conidia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Exclusive production of ascospores is characteristic of the Ascomycetes class, which shows sexual reproduction — the opposite of the Deuteromycetes' defining feature.
  • Exclusive production of basidiospores is characteristic of Basidiomycetes, an entirely different fungal class from Deuteromycetes.
  • Broad, aseptate hyphae are characteristic of the primitive class Phycomycetes, not specifically Deuteromycetes.
Know More
  • A fungus showing sexual reproduction (alone or with asexual) is called a perfect fungus.
  • Saccharomyces cerevisiae is an example of a perfect fungus.
  • Basidiospores develop on club-shaped structures called basidia.
  • Ascomycete asci are enclosed within a perithecium in filamentous forms.

posts.post_title: Category of mycosis in which the etiological…
posts.post_content: Mycoses in which the agent invades deep tissue and creates symptoms resembling other diseases of the affected organ (e.g. histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis) are classified as?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Systemic mycoses

Systemic mycoses invade deep tissue, are the most serious category, and may also have cutaneous manifestations.

Correct Option Explanation

Examples include candidiasis, cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, geotrichosis and blastomycosis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Superficial mycoses are confined to the outermost skin/hair layers and are the least serious category, e.g. Trichosporon cutaneum.
  • Cutaneous mycoses involve keratin invasion in skin, hair and nails (e.g. dermatophytes, Candida), more serious than superficial but less than systemic.
  • Subcutaneous mycoses invade primarily muscle tissue (e.g. Rhinosporidium, Sporothrix), more serious than cutaneous but distinct from the deep-organ systemic category.
Know More
  • Dermatophytosis is an exception, being a contagious/zoonotic fungal disease.
  • Fungal infections often produce a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response.
  • Cell-mediated immunity is usually more important than humoral immunity against fungi.
  • Prolonged antibiotic therapy commonly predisposes to intestinal candidiasis.

posts.post_title: Specialized hypha structure bearing a sporan…
posts.post_content: The specialized hypha bearing a sporangium, from which asexual sporangiospores are released (e.g. in Rhizopus), is called?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sporangiophore

A sporangiophore is the specialised hypha bearing a sporangium.

Correct Option Explanation

The persisting dome-shaped upper portion of the sporangiophore, remaining after spore release, is called the columella.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A conidiophore is a stalk-like branch of mycelium on which conidia develop (e.g. Penicillium), a different structure from the sporangium-bearing sporangiophore.
  • The columella is the dome-shaped remnant of the sporangiophore after sporangiospore release, not the structure bearing the sporangium itself.
  • A perithecium is the tightly meshed hyphal network enclosing asci in filamentous Ascomycetes, unrelated to sporangium-bearing structures.
Know More
  • Sporangiospores are produced within a closed, often spherical sporangium.
  • Conidia may be classified as macroconidia or microconidia based on size.
  • Perithecia enclose asci in the filamentous type of Ascomycetes.
  • Basidiospores develop on a specialised club-like structure called a basidium.

posts.post_title: Species most commonly infecting cattle and s…
posts.post_content: Among the zoophilic dermatophytes, which species predominantly affects cattle and sheep?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Trichophyton verrucosum

Trichophyton verrucosum predominantly affects cattle and sheep.

Correct Option Explanation

Mild inflammatory reactions are typically seen with T. verrucosum infection in calves, and cultures suspected of T. verrucosum are incubated at 37°C.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • T. mentagrophytes affects all domestic animals broadly and causes severe reactions especially in dogs, not specifically cattle/sheep.
  • M. canis predominantly affects dogs, cats, primates and horses, not cattle/sheep specifically.
  • M. gypseum is a geophilic pathogen mainly affecting dogs, cats, horses and humans, not the specific cattle/sheep pathogen.
Know More
  • T. equinum is the classic dermatophyte of horses.
  • T. gallinae affects fowl, causing fowl favus (white comb).
  • M. nanum affects swine and humans.
  • Zoophilic infections spread animal to human; geophilic infections spread soil to animal/human.

posts.post_title: Genus predominantly producing macroconidia a…
posts.post_content: As a general rule, which dermatophyte genus predominantly produces macroconidia, while Trichophyton species predominantly produce microconidia?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Microsporum

Most Microsporum species predominantly produce macroconidia, while most Trichophyton species predominantly produce microconidia.

Correct Option Explanation

Shape, size, structure, arrangement and abundance of conidia are important diagnostic criteria for species identification, though this rule is not absolute.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Epidermophyton is a dermatophyte genus but is not described as the macroconidia-predominant genus in this general rule.
  • Geotrichum is associated with arthrospore formation (via mycelial disarticulation), not the macroconidia-predominant dermatophyte pattern.
  • Chrysosporium is not the genus described in this classic macroconidia-vs-microconidia rule for dermatophytes.
Know More
  • Hyphal peculiarities include spirals, nodules, rackets and chandeliers.
  • Arthroconidia in tissue can remain infectious for years.
  • Only M. canis among animal dermatophytes produces green fluorescence under Wood's light.
  • Fluorescence is due to a tryptophan metabolite.

posts.post_title: Hair invasion pattern where arthroconidia de…
posts.post_content: The pattern of dermatophyte hair invasion in which arthroconidia develop within the hair shaft only, with the cuticle remaining intact, is called?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Endothrix

Endothrix invasion shows arthroconidia developing within the hair shaft only, with an intact cuticle.

Correct Option Explanation

In contrast, ectothrix invasion shows arthroconidia outside the hair shaft with hyphae inside, and cuticle destruction.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ectothrix is the opposite pattern, with external arthroconidia and cuticle destruction, not the intact-cuticle internal pattern described.
  • 'Favic type' and 'mosaic type' are not the standard terminology used in this text for the two hair invasion patterns (endothrix/ectothrix).
Know More
  • Hair invasion begins with spore germination near a follicular orifice.
  • Growing hair carries hyphae/conidia to the surface, often causing the hair to break off.
  • In hairless skin, growth pattern predominates with M. nanum and T. rubrum.
  • Specimens for culture should be collected from the edge of the lesion, the most active infection site.

posts.post_title: Selective medium used to culture dermatophyt…
posts.post_content: Which medium, containing selective agents like cycloheximide, gentamicin/tetracycline or chloramphenicol, turns red as dermatophytes grow on it?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Dermatophyte test medium (DTM)

DTM turns red as dermatophytes grow, aiding presumptive identification.

Correct Option Explanation

Although selective, other molds may still grow on DTM, so identification should always be confirmed by microscopy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Plain Sabouraud dextrose agar supports dermatophyte growth but does not have the colour-change indicator system described for DTM.
  • Bird seed agar is selective for Cryptococcus neoformans, an unrelated fungal organism, not for dermatophytes.
  • Lowenstein-Jensen medium is used for Mycobacterium isolation, unrelated to dermatophyte culture.
Know More
  • Dermatophyte cultures require incubation at 25-30°C for up to 4 weeks.
  • T. verrucosum suspected samples are incubated at 37°C.
  • Sabouraud dextrose agar has an acidic pH of 5.6, mildly bacteriostatic.
  • Cycloheximide is used at 500 µg/ml for selectivity.

posts.post_title: Systemic drug of choice for treating severe …
posts.post_content: Which orally administered systemic antifungal drug, incorporated into keratin to render skin resistant to infection, is most beneficial for treating severe dermatophytosis in small animals?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Griseofulvin

Griseofulvin, given orally, is most beneficial for severe dermatophyte infections in small animals.

Correct Option Explanation

Since the fungus is shed with dead skin, prolonged therapy (at least a month, or two weeks minimum) is required, particularly for nail infections; Gentles (1958) first reported its oral use.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Amphotericin B is a systemic antifungal typically used for deep/systemic mycoses (e.g. Cryptococcus, Blastomyces), not the first-line drug described for dermatophytosis here.
  • Nystatin is primarily a topical/enteric antifungal for Candida, not the systemic dermatophytosis drug described.
  • Potassium iodide is used to treat sporotrichosis and actinobacillosis (wooden tongue), not dermatophytosis.
Know More
  • Ketoconazole and fluconazole may also be used but are more expensive.
  • Sabouraud published detailed dermatophyte studies in 1910.
  • The sexual state of some dermatophytes was identified in 1959, placing them in Ascomycetes.
  • Dermatophyte infection is not fatal but causes significant economic loss.

posts.post_title: Characteristic appearance of avian crop myco…
posts.post_content: In acute avian moniliasis (crop mycosis), the crop wall becomes thickened and covered by a corrugated pseudomembrane, giving which characteristic appearance?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Turkey-towelling appearance

The corrugated yellowish-grey necrotic pseudomembrane gives a characteristic 'turkey-towelling' appearance.

Correct Option Explanation

Lesions are confined mainly to the crop, less frequently invading the mouth, oesophagus, proventriculus, gizzard and intestine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Onion ring' appearance describes the concentric caseous layers of Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis lymphadenitis, unrelated to avian candidiasis.
  • 'Medusa head' describes B. anthracis colony morphology, unrelated to crop mycosis lesions.
  • 'Frosted glass' also describes B. anthracis colonial appearance on agar, unrelated to this avian mucosal lesion.
Know More
  • Candida albicans is also called moniliasis or candidosis.
  • In swine, C. albicans causes stomach ulcers and cutaneous candidiasis.
  • In puppies, kittens, calves and foals, it causes mycotic stomatitis and enteritis.
  • Alimentary tract candidiasis is often called thrush.

posts.post_title: Test demonstrating germ tube formation chara…
posts.post_content: Which rapid diagnostic test involves suspending a Candida colony in serum and incubating at 37°C for 2-3 hours to observe small thin-walled tube-like projections?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Germ tube test

The germ tube (serum tube) test demonstrates thin-walled tube projections characteristic of C. albicans within 2-3 hrs.

Correct Option Explanation

Sheep, bovine, rabbit or human serum can be used, with examination under phase contrast or high-power light microscopy for the diagnostic germ tubes.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Nagler's reaction demonstrates C. perfringens lecithinase activity, an unrelated bacterial (not fungal) test.
  • The CAMP test identifies group B streptococci or other CAMP-positive bacteria, unrelated to Candida diagnosis.
  • Ascoli's test is a precipitation test for anthrax antigen, unrelated to fungal diagnosis.
Know More
  • Dalmau's technique demonstrates chlamydospores on corn meal-Tween 80 agar.
  • BiGGy agar (Bismuth-sulphite-glucose-glycine-yeast) helps isolate and identify C. albicans.
  • C. albicans strongly reduces bismuth sulphite to bismuth sulphide, giving brownish colonies.
  • C. albicans is the only species among those compared that produces chlamydospores on corn meal agar.

posts.post_title: Most effective drug for treating systemic ca…
posts.post_content: Which antifungal drug is considered the most effective treatment for systemic candidiasis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Amphotericin B

Amphotericin B is the most effective drug for treating systemic candidiasis.

Correct Option Explanation

Ketoconazole and clotrimazole have also been effective for mucocutaneous candidiasis, while nystatin is more commonly used for superficial/enteric forms.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Nystatin (Mycostatin) is administered in feed or the mammary gland for candidiasis/mastitis but is not the most effective systemic drug described.
  • Griseofulvin is the drug of choice for dermatophytosis, not systemic candidiasis.
  • Potassium iodide treats sporotrichosis and actinobacillosis, unrelated to systemic candidiasis.
Know More
  • Candida possesses adhesins consisting of fibrillar peptide mannans.
  • C. albicans cell wall glycoproteins have endotoxin-like activity.
  • Disseminated (systemic) candidiasis is more common in immunosuppressed animals.
  • C. albicans appears purple-blue in Gram-stained smears.

posts.post_title: Fermentation pattern that best distinguishes…
posts.post_content: Which biochemical feature is unique to C. albicans among the compared Candida species (C. albicans, C. tropicalis, C. pseudotropicalis, C. parapsilosis)?

_aimcq_options.text: Chlamydospore formation on corn meal agar
Acid and gas production from glucose

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chlamydospore formation on corn meal agar

Only C. albicans is positive for chlamydospore formation on corn meal agar among the species compared.

Correct Option Explanation

All four species ferment glucose with acid and gas, so this alone does not differentiate them; chlamydospore production is the unique distinguishing feature.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acid and gas production from glucose is common to all four Candida species compared, not unique to C. albicans.
  • Ability to grow at 37°C is a shared property among pathogenic Candida species generally, not a distinguishing feature.
  • Yeast morphology on Sabouraud agar is shared broadly across Candida species, not a specific differentiator for C. albicans.
Know More
  • C. albicans and C. tropicalis produce colonies on BiGGy agar with different colour reactions after 72 hrs.
  • C. tropicalis shows diffuse blackening of the medium, unlike C. albicans.
  • C. parapsilosis is implicated in bovine abortion.
  • C. rugosa has been implicated in pyometra in a mare.

posts.post_title: Characteristic appearance of rhinosporidiosi…
posts.post_content: The nasal polyps of rhinosporidiosis, caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi, are classically described with which descriptive appearance?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Strawberry-like/mulberry mass

Rhinosporidiosis polyps are classically described as a strawberry-like or mulberry mass.

Correct Option Explanation

These pink to deep red, sessile or pedunculated polyps are vascular and friable, bleeding easily upon manipulation, and can obstruct the respiratory tract causing asphyxia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Onion ring' mass describes Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis lymphadenitis, an unrelated bacterial lesion.
  • 'Cauliflower-like verrucous' lesions are more typical of certain other chronic granulomatous conditions, not the specific strawberry/mulberry description of rhinosporidiosis.
  • 'Grape-cluster' describes the arrangement of Staphylococcus (from which the genus name is derived), unrelated to rhinosporidiosis lesion morphology.
Know More
  • Rhinosporidiosis was first described in man by Seeberi (1910).
  • The natural habitat is associated with stagnant water.
  • The disease is most common in India and Sri Lanka.
  • About 90% of infections involve the nose of male animals.

posts.post_title: Life cycle structure of Rhinosporidium seebe…
posts.post_content: The thick-walled structure of Rhinosporidium seeberi, measuring 100-450 µm in diameter and containing up to several thousand endospores, is called?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sporangium

The sporangium, 100-450 µm in diameter, contains up to several thousand endospores in the life cycle of R. seeberi.

Correct Option Explanation

Mature sporangiospores, approximately 7-9 µm in size, escape through a pore that develops in the sporangial wall, beginning as a round endospore (6-10 µm) that grows into this sporangium.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • An ascus is the sac-like structure producing sexual ascospores in Ascomycetes (e.g. Saccharomyces), a different fungal reproductive structure unrelated to Rhinosporidium.
  • A basidium is the club-shaped structure producing basidiospores in Basidiomycetes, unrelated to Rhinosporidium's life cycle.
  • A perithecium is the hyphal network enclosing asci in filamentous Ascomycetes, an unrelated fungal structure.
Know More
  • Infection is typically limited to the mucosal epithelium.
  • No evidence exists of animal-to-animal or animal-to-man transmission.
  • Injury and inhalation of contaminated dust may both play a role in transmission.
  • Besides the nose, infection can affect the palpebral conjunctivae, skin, ear, genitals and rectum.

posts.post_title: Selective medium for isolating Cryptococcus …
posts.post_content: Which selective medium, containing Guizotia abyssinica (niger) seeds, is used for isolating Cryptococcus neoformans, which produces melanin-pigmented brown colonies?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bird seed agar

Bird seed agar (containing niger seeds with di- and polyphenolic compounds) selects for C. neoformans, producing dark brown pigmented colonies.

Correct Option Explanation

This pigmentation results from C. neoformans's use of creatinine and a unique diphenol oxidase enzyme, which also contributes to its virulence.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cetrimide agar is selective for Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an unrelated bacterial organism.
  • Purple agar differentiates S. aureus from S. intermedius, unrelated to Cryptococcus.
  • PLET medium is selective for B. anthracis, unrelated to fungal isolation.
Know More
  • The natural reservoir is pigeon faeces and soil contaminated by avian excreta.
  • The organism can survive in pigeon droppings for over a year.
  • C. neoformans can grow at temperatures up to 40°C, unlike most other Cryptococcus species.
  • C. neoformans is highly urease positive.

posts.post_title: Stain used to demonstrate the capsule of Cry…
posts.post_content: Which negative staining method demonstrates the large mucopolysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans as a clear halo around the yeast cell?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: India ink / Nigrosin stain

India ink or Nigrosin staining demonstrates the budding yeast with a large capsule, appearing as a clear halo.

Correct Option Explanation

Lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) can also be used; PAS-haematoxylin staining outlines the yeast cell but not the capsule itself, which appears clear.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The Ziehl-Neelsen stain is used for acid-fast organisms like Mycobacterium, not for demonstrating fungal capsules.
  • Gram stain alone shows C. neoformans as Gram-positive yeast cells but does not specifically highlight the capsule as a negative-stain technique does.
  • Sudan black B stains B. anthracis spores, unrelated to Cryptococcus capsule demonstration.
Know More
  • C. neoformans has two varieties: var. neoformans (serotypes A, D) and var. gattii (serotypes B, C).
  • The teleomorph (sexual state) of serotypes A/D is Filobasidiella neoformans.
  • C. neoformans is a member of the fungi imperfecti.
  • Amphotericin B is the drug of choice for cryptococcosis treatment.

posts.post_title: Cause of cryptococcal mastitis in cattle
posts.post_content: Cryptococcal mastitis in cattle, in which milk becomes grey, white, highly viscid and mucoid, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cryptococcus neoformans

Cryptococcus neoformans causes cryptococcal mastitis in cattle.

Correct Option Explanation

Mild infections may show no clinical signs except udder swelling, while severe cases mimic bacterial mastitis with fever, swelling and firm udder tissue.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Histoplasma capsulatum causes histoplasmosis, primarily a pulmonary/reticuloendothelial disease, not specifically cattle mastitis.
  • Blastomyces dermatitidis causes blastomycosis affecting lungs, skin and bones, not the specific mastitis syndrome described.
  • Coccidioides immitis causes coccidioidomycosis, primarily a respiratory disease, unrelated to bovine mastitis.

This is distinct from A. flavus and A. parasiticus (which produce aflatoxins) and A. ochraceus (which produces ochratoxin).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A. flavus and A. parasiticus are the classic aflatoxin-producing species, not sterigmatocystin producers.
  • A. ochraceus produces ochratoxin, a different mycotoxin from sterigmatocystin.
  • A. niger and A. fumigatus are primarily associated with mycotic infections (fungus balls, mycotic abortion) rather than being highlighted as the classic sterigmatocystin producers.
Know More
  • Fusarium roseum produces trichothecane (T-2) toxin.
  • Penicillium citrinum produces citrinin.
  • Toxigenic fungi produce mycotoxins only under specific environmental conditions.
  • The susceptibility of crops to mould infection depends on suitable substrates.

posts.post_content: Aspergillus fumigatus, the primary cause of mycotic abortion in cattle, typically reaches the placenta via which two main routes of infection?

_aimcq_options.text: Inhalation into lungs or ingestion, with haematogenous spread to placenta

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inhalation into lungs or ingestion, with haematogenous spread to placenta

Infection mainly occurs by inhalation into lungs or ingestion, with the organism carried to the placenta via the bloodstream from respiratory or digestive tract lesions.

Correct Option Explanation

This causes a slowly developing fungal placentitis over one to two months, interfering with foetal nutrition and resulting in foetal death and abortion, most commonly at 6-7 months of gestation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct venereal transmission is not the described route for A. fumigatus mycotic abortion; the organism spreads haematogenously from respiratory/digestive lesions instead.
  • Transovarial transmission is a route described for certain tick-borne pathogens (e.g. some Rickettsiales), not for Aspergillus mycotic abortion.
  • Direct skin penetration only does not reflect the described pathogenesis, which specifically involves inhalation/ingestion and haematogenous spread.
Know More
  • The aborted foetus shows ringworm-type skin lesions on the head and neck.
  • The placenta is thickened, haemorrhagic, oedematous and necrotic.
  • Chronic infection may cause purulent vaginitis, cervicitis and endometritis, leading to infertility.
  • High humidity and temperature during hay/straw storage encourage mould growth, the infection source.
